title: the people we met the hotel you stayed at (relative clauses 2)
subtitle: The bag he is carrying is very heavy.
summary: Leave out that, who or which when it is the object: the people we met, the hotel you stayed at.

lesson.heading: The bag he is carrying
lesson.text: A man is walking along with a very big bag. He is hot and tired. Kate is reading a letter: 'Congratulations - you have won £50,000!' For each one we can say two sentences or one sentence. In the one sentence we do not need **that** at all.

examples.text: The man is carrying a bag. **It**'s very heavy.
**The bag (that) he is carrying** is very heavy.
Kate won some money. What is she going to do with **it**?
What is Kate going to do with **the money (that) she won**?

lesson.heading: subject + verb + object -> one phrase
rows: the bag (that) the man was carrying

lesson.heading: You do not need that / who / which
lesson.text: When **that**, **who** or **which** is the object, you can leave it out. This is very common in speaking.

examples.text: Did you find **the books you wanted**?
examples.note: or the books that you wanted

examples.text: **The people we met** were very friendly.
examples.note: or the people who we met

examples.text: **The film we saw** was very good.
examples.wrong: The film we saw it was

lesson.heading: Sometimes there is a preposition
lesson.text: The verb often has a preposition (**to**, **in**, **at**, **about**, **for**). The preposition stays with the verb, at the end.

examples.text: Eve is talking **to** a man. -> Do you know **the man Eve is talking to**?
We stayed **at** a hotel. -> **The hotel we stayed at** was near the station.
I told you **about** some books. -> These are **the books I told you about**.
examples.wrong: the books I told you about them

lesson.heading: (a place) where ...
lesson.text: For a place you can also use **where**. Then you do not need a preposition at the end.

examples.text: **The hotel where we stayed** was near the station.
What's the name of the restaurant **where** you had dinner?

left.label: object - you can leave who/that out
left.text: There is another subject after it.

right.label: subject - you must use who/that/which
right.text: There is a verb straight after it.
examples: I met a woman **who can speak** six languages.
Jack was wearing a hat **that was** too big for him.

lesson.text: Do not say the object twice. Say *The film we saw was very good*, not ~~The film we saw it was very good~~.

exercises.prompt: You cooked a meal. It was excellent. The meal ___ was excellent.
exercises.explanation: you cooked is the object part, so we do not need that.

exercises.prompt: I'm wearing shoes. They aren't very comfortable. The shoes ___ aren't very comfortable.
exercises.explanation: The shoes I'm wearing ... - no that is necessary here.

exercises.prompt: Match the two halves of each sentence.

exercises.statement: The people we met were very friendly.
exercises.explanation: Correct. who is the object here, so we can leave it out.

exercises.prompt: Your friend was looking for some keys. You ask: Did you find the keys you were looking ___?
exercises.explanation: look for keeps its preposition at the end of the question.

exercises.prompt: Helen took some photographs. Have you seen them? Make one question.
exercises.answer: Have you seen the photographs Helen took?
exercises.explanation: the photographs is the object, so we do not need that.

exercises.prompt: The film we saw ___ very good.
exercises.explanation: We do not say the object twice: The film we saw was very good.

exercises.prompt: Sarah lives in a village. You ask her: How big is the village ___ live?
exercises.explanation: For a place we can say where: the village where you live.

exercises.statement: These are the books I told you about them.
exercises.explanation: These are the books I told you about. Do not add them at the end.

exercises.prompt: I was carrying a bag. It was very heavy. Make one sentence.
exercises.answer: The bag I was carrying was very heavy.
exercises.explanation: The bag is the object of was carrying, so that is not necessary.

exercises.prompt: We invited some people to dinner. They didn't come. The people ___ to dinner didn't come.
exercises.explanation: The people is the object of invited, so we can leave who out.

exercises.statement: I met a woman can speak six languages.
exercises.explanation: I met a woman who can speak six languages. Here who is the subject, so you must use it.
